Learning Path: Data Management Professionals

Welcome! This learning path is designed for County of Santa Clara professionals who are interested in learning more about data management best practices and key concepts. Please consult a Subject Matter Expert (SME) for clarification on these topics, as this wiki may not cover all necessary details.

Level 1: Foundational Concepts

This section covers some of the core principles of data management along with the key roles involved in this process.

Data Lifecycle Management

Defines a series of stages that data goes through from its creation to its eventual archival or deletion, typically involving data storage, processing, analysis, interpretation.

Data at Rest

Data at rest refers to data that is stored on a physical or cloud-based system and is not actively being used or transferred. This can include data stored on hard drives, flash drives, databases, archives, servers, and other storage media.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 18:58 · admin

Data in Transit

Data in transit refers to the movement of data from one location to another over the internet or a private network. This includes actions such as sending email attachments, uploading information to a web application, transferring data between databases, or collecting user-submitted data from a website into a county system.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:01 · admin

Data Owner

Data owners define how data should be used and shared, while ensuring that all practices align with legal and organizational requirements. They determine who has permission to access, edit, or delete the data. Data owners define data governance policies and appropriate safeguards to protect data from unauthorized access or malicious activity. They are also accountable for ensuring compliance with applicable regulations, such as GDPR, HIPAA, and County-specific data policies.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:07 · admin

Data Steward

A Data Steward is responsible for the day-to-day management and governance of data. They execute data governance policies set by data owners. Data Stewards make sure the data is complete, accurate, consistent, and is well documented. They also control who can access the data and how it can be used or shared, keeping it secure. Other tasks may include cleaning up messy or outdated data and organizing the data.

Controller

The natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body which, alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data; where the purposes and means of such processing are determined by Union or Member State law, the controller or the specific criteria for its nomination may be provided for by Union or Member State law.

Level 2: Infrastructure & Maintenance

A short overview of key concepts and infrastructure involved in storing, managing, and moving data across systems.

Cloud Storage

A service which allows digital data to be stored in remote servers in off-site locations. Often times, these remote servers are managed by a 3rd party cloud service provider.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 18:50 · admin

Data Integrity

Data integrity means making sure that data is accurate and complete at any point during its lifecycle. It also ensures data is consistent, so that it stays the same and up to date across different systems. Data integrity ensures the reliability of data, which allows people to trust the data being used for reports and important decision making.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:11 · admin

Data Catalog

A document that lists all the datasets available in a department or organization. For each dataset, the catalog describes what kind of content the dataset contains, where the dataset is stored, and how it can be accessed. If a dataset is restricted in access, the data catalog will provide instructions on how to request permission to gain access.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 18:58 · admin

Data Migration

Permanently moving data from one storage location, system, or format to another. This process often follows best practices set by federal agencies like NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology). Some key aspects of data migration involve keeping the data secure, ensuring data accuracy, minimizing downtime, creating clear documentation, and testing to ensure everything works after the migration.

Data Synchronization

The process of keeping data consistent and up to date across different systems or storage locations. This is critical in places where data is used by multiple departments or services, as it helps to avoid errors and confusion.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:10 · admin

Data Interoperability

Data formatted in a way which allows it be easily shared, understood, and used across different systems in different organizations. To achieve data interoperability, data must follow shared standards so that all systems can interpret the data in the same way.

Level 3: Data Governance and Compliance

A brief introduction into some of the policies and safeguards employed to ensure County data is stored responsibly, recoverable in emergencies, and maintained in compliance with Federal, State, and County regulations.

Data Retention Policy

A set of rules which determines how long data should be kept before it is archived or deleted. It applies to the final step of the data lifecycle. These rules ensure that data is not stored longer than necessary.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:08 · admin

Disaster Recovery

A set of procedures set in place to help restore IT systems, data, and operations after a disruption. The goal is to prevent data loss and minimize downtime so that critical services can quickly return to normal.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 19:12 · admin

Personally Identifiable Information (PII)

Any data that can be used alone or with other information to identify an individual. This includes personal data like the first and last name, mailing address, date of birth, gender, race, religion, driver's license number, social security number, and medical records.

Some types of PII are direct identifiers because they are unique to one person. An example is someone's driver's license number. Other types of PII are called indirect identifiers, meaning they are not unique to one person. An example is date of birth. Multiple indirect identifiers strung together could identify a person.
